title: Will there be a bilateral ceasefire in the Russo-Ukrainian conflict before 2027?
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as Yes if a bilateral ceasefire in the Russo-Ukrainian conflict has gone into effect during 2026. The ceasefire must either

* last a minimum of 30 consecutive days entirely during 2026

or

* be intended to last a minimum of 30 days (or indefinitely), as specified by the agreement text or joint statement, even if it is immediately violated.
fine_print:
A ceasefire will qualify if it is mutually agreed by Russia and Ukraine and applies to all kinetic fighting against the other by both sides.

A ceasefire will have considered to have lasted if both Russia and Ukraine agree that it has remained in effect and full scale fighting has not occurred. Minor ceasefire violations, while both sides agree to continue the ceasefire, will not impact this question.

comments.author: josheee
comments.text: The crux here is the 30-consecutive-day hold, not the announcement of a ceasefire. Talks remain stalled on Donbas (Russia wants all of it, Ukraine will not cede it), and the ceasefires announced on this front have tended to fracture within days. Getting a bilateral deal to both take effect AND survive 30 unbroken days entirely within 2026, even under heavy US deadline pressure, is a demanding compound bar. That is why I am at 10%, a bit below the community: I suspect the crowd is partly pricing the chance a ceasefire is announced rather than the narrower chance one holds a full month. The main tail is a rushed US-brokered settlement in H2 that both exhausted sides observe for an initial 30 days.

comments.author: GOLDEN-BLUE
comments.text:
Russia's spring offensive appears to have failed completely:

![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJUYiQ_XQAAs7F9?format=jpg\&name=4096x4096)Instead Ukraine has successfully retaken parts of Zaporizhzhia and Dnipro oblasts, marking the first territorial reversal for Russia since 2023. Ukraine is also now able to strike much of the land corridor connecting Crimea to mainland Russia, and this is having a predictably poor effect on Russian logistics in the southern region.

On one hand: Russia is the binding constraint on any lasting ceasefire and these operational failures, in addition to slowly mounting economic problems and dwindling pool of willing recruits, should increase the chance of a ceasefire, if only to allow them a month or three's breathing space. On the other hand: Russia has previously reacted to large reversals e.g. 2022 counteroffensives by escalating, in that case via annexation, mobilisation and nuclear signalling, however this reversal has been much smaller in scale plus the cons likely outweighed the pros for the previous mobilisation.

Overall a lasting ceasefire is only likely to be agreed when both a) Putin realises that Russia cannot keep grinding forward infinitely AND b) he opts to de-escalate rather than escalate. The chance of a) increases exponentially the longer Russia stops gaining territory while still incurring high casualties. The chance of b) is very difficult to forecast however it's worth noting that he has generally chosen escalation in the past, as until Feb 2022 it always worked out for him.

comments.author: RuslanBes
comments.text:
Article at the [Economist](https://www.economist.com/leaders/2026/02/19/vladimir-putin-is-caught-in-a-vice-of-his-own-making) (you need to login to read it but the article itself is free). Basically confirms everything me and @(Zaldath) were discussing here.

Summary (From AI, and I improved it)

#### 
**1. The Battlefield Stalemate**

The front line has a 10-30km "kill zone" heavily monitored by drones, so it's impossible for Russian forces to mass equipment or troops without being destroyed. Meaning - they can't get a breakthrough.

**2. The Manpower and Economic Crisis**

Russia is now losing soldiers faster than it can replace them. Meaning heavier costs for the economy to keep the war ongoing.


#### **3. The Illusions of Peace**

* **Unacceptable Terms:** Any realistic peace deal will not grant Putin the territory he needs to declare a domestic victory.
* **Ukrainian Resilience:** Ukraine is now less dependent on American financing and intelligence meaning there is less leverage from the US on the Ukraine (we likely already crossed the peak of their pressure on Ukraine
* Also: For Ukraine **to surrender its best-defended ground would be a strategic disaster**.

#### **4. The Domestic Danger of Ending the War**

Ironically, peace might be more dangerous to Putin than war. The Russian economy has been entirely rewired for conflict, with defense now making up 8% of the GDP.

comments.author: RuslanBes
comments.text:
@(Zaldath) Yes, inertia is my answer. [Sunk cost fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunk_cost).

It's very similar to Hitler's campaign in early 1942 where he was stopped 40km from Moscow and then poured more and more forces believing that USSR almost collapsed and victory is within reach.

Different scale, same psychology.

comments.author: wd28
comments.text:
@(RuslanBes) Great analysis, thanks! I think you're too optimistic about both Russian and Ukrainian economy, and, unfortunately, about economical problems leading to the end of war. I used to think this war will end when one side runs out of money, but now it looks like the Russian joke "- Dad, vodka prices are surging, does it mean you will drink less? - No, my boy, it means you will eat less" is an accurate description of what will happen.

In Russia, the canary to watch is a construction sector. It heavily depends on credit money, and can't function at current rate even with rapid price increases. Largest Russian developer company, Samolet (Airplane), asks for a government support of 50 bn rub (600 mn usd) *for operating expenses*, claiming it will bankrupt otherwise. This is probably just the tip of the iceberg, and this year we'll see either multibillion dollar government bailouts of key construction companies, or chain of bankrupcies that will bring down several large weak banks as well (MKB comes to mind, but there will be others). Government is likely to choose the first path, and this will drain the FNB you mention very quickly.

In Ukraine, there is not much of economy to speak about outside of external life support. GDP that is *not* government spending is less than in, say, Angola. This did not matter much,  because entire non-military budget was covered by EU, WB and IMF grants and loans, but 2026 budget is different. Last year many support measures were announced, such as 50% wage increase for teachers, 2mn uah (50k usd) one-time support for people with home on occupied territories, free train tickets for all citizens (limited by 3000km), etc. They look like populist measures to sustain government popularity (maybe in preparation for election?), and they drove the projected deficit upwards from 40-50 bn usd to 60-70 bn usd. They probably expected to fund it with seized Russian assets, but those didn't materialize. Furthermore, the 90 bn eur package is actually worse than what was given before. Formally, it is a two-year package, but it is likely to run dry before the years end. Most important is that it is not 90 bn eur to sustain Ukrainian economy, only 30 bn is allocated for that purpose, and 60 bn is allocated for military procurement from EU (which is quite a sum, definitely more than Russia's, US allocated 140 bn eur for military procurement in 2025). That 30 bn is falling short of Ukrainian needs even if we assume it will all be spent in one year, and account for support via WB and IMF. Hence, the government must choose between backtracking on those commitments or devaluing them by devaluing uah. I think it will be second one, as it allows to shift blame, but also more felt by population.

All those considerations do not stop *both* governments from negotiating in bad faith (yes, this is where we disagree), so the war is likely to continue regardless of how much worse it will be for the population
